w: Bolted to the Royal Observatory's gate since 1852, this dial ran on electric pulses wired from a master clock inside -- Charles Shepherd's 'sympathetic clock' network. Likely the first place the public could read Greenwich Mean Time, shown on an unusual 24-hour face; the day once began at noon, not midnight.
s: First public clock to show Greenwich Mean Time
_facts: Installed 1852 by Charles Shepherd
Ran on electric pulses from a master clock inside the Observatory
Rare 24-hour analogue dial; originally showed astronomical time starting at noon

w: An 11-foot zinc cosmonaut stands on a globe by the Thames path -- a replica of Anatoly Novikov's original in Lyubertsy, where Gagarin trained as a foundry apprentice before he became the first man in space. Roscosmos gave it to the British Council in 2011, marking fifty years since that first flight.
s: First man in space, cast in zinc, gifted by Roscosmos
_facts: 3.5m zinc statue, a replica of the Lyubertsy original by Anatoly Novikov
Gift from Russian space agency Roscosmos to the British Council
Marked the 50th anniversary of Gagarin's 1961 flight

w: Christopher Wren's Greenwich Hospital, raised 1696-1712 for wounded and retired sailors, still frames the long river axis he preserved to keep the view from the older Queen's House unbroken. It trained naval officers until 1998; UNESCO now calls the ensemble the finest and most dramatically sited in the British Isles.
s: Wren's naval hospital, heart of Maritime Greenwich
_facts: Built 1696-1712 by Christopher Wren as Greenwich Hospital for the Royal Navy
Wren preserved the river sightline to the earlier Queen's House
Used as the Royal Naval College 1873-1998; now the core of the Maritime Greenwich World Heritage Site

w: Joseph Kay built this riverside tavern in 1837 on the site of an older pub, right against the Old Royal Naval College. It ran until 1915, then did time as a working men's club and flats before reopening as a pub in 1965. Grade II listed since 1973, it sits inside the Maritime Greenwich World Heritage boundary.
s: 1837 riverside pub beside the Naval College
_facts: Built 1837 by architect Joseph Kay
Closed 1915; used as a working men's club and housing before reopening as a pub in 1965
Grade II listed 1973; within the Maritime Greenwich World Heritage Site

w: Nothing remains above ground of the hunting lodge Henry VIII kept on this hill, built by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester and long known as Duke Humphrey's Tower. Henry supposedly used it to house his mistresses, an easy ride from Greenwich Palace below. The Royal Observatory now occupies the site.
s: Henry VIII's vanished hilltop hunting lodge
_facts: Originally Duke Humphrey's Tower, built by Humphrey, Duke of Gloucester
Used by Henry VIII as a hunting lodge, reputedly to house mistresses
Site now occupied by the Royal Observatory, Greenwich

w: A 45-ton bronze cone sunk into Greenwich Park, tilted to the Observatory's latitude and sliced parallel to the celestial equator -- built 50 metres east of the prime meridian. Inside, three lasers sweep a 4,000-pixel strip across the dome sixty times a second. It opened in 2007, funded by philanthropist Peter Harrison.
s: Bronze cone tilted to the sky, 50m from the meridian
_facts: 45-ton bronze-clad truncated cone, opened 25 May 2007
Sides aligned to Greenwich's latitude and the celestial equator
Funded by a 3.25 million grant from the Peter Harrison Foundation

w: An Edwardian Baroque hall in Woolwich's Bathway Quarter, it ran the Metropolitan Borough of Woolwich until 1965, then became Greenwich Council's headquarters. Grade II* listed and still the borough's register office, it is one of London's rarer surviving examples of the Edwardian Baroque civic style.
s: Edwardian Baroque seat of old Woolwich borough
_facts: Seat of the Metropolitan Borough of Woolwich until 1965
Became headquarters of the Greenwich London Borough Council
Grade II* listed; rare Edwardian Baroque town hall; still the borough register office

w: General Wolfe stands at the crest of Greenwich Park, given by Canada in gratitude for his capture of Quebec in 1759 -- the battle that killed him. The sculptor, R. Tait McKenzie, was Canadian; fittingly, the statue was unveiled in 1930 by the Marquis de Montcalm, descendant of the French general Wolfe had defeated.
s: Canada's gift to the general who took Quebec, and died
_facts: Bronze statue by Canadian sculptor R. Tait McKenzie, a gift of the Canadian people
Commemorates Wolfe's capture of Quebec at the 1759 Battle of the Plains of Abraham, where he died
Unveiled 1930 by the Marquis de Montcalm, descendant of the opposing French general
